findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State in Root cause/Approach, and in the docs/concurrency.md update, that on Windows git_locking's git-op and fetch-coordination locks are no-ops (fcntl is None), so a detached sweep relies on the store write lock and git's bounded retries for git-level coordination.
evidence: Plan: "Every module on these paths guards `import fcntl` with a None fallback (`lock_kernel`, `git_locking`, `repo_snapshot`)."
src/rebar/_store/git_locking.py:191-193: `if lock_path is None or fcntl is None: yield; return` (git-op lock skipped)
src/rebar/_store/git_locking.py:326-328: `if common is None or fcntl is None: yield; return` (fetch coordination lock skipped)
git_locking docstrings call both locks advisory, 'not load-bearing', with the bounded git/CAS retry as the correctness net.
findings.finding: The plan offers "Every module on these paths guards `import fcntl` with a None fallback" as evidence that the detached child is now safe on Windows. The guard does stop the import from crashing. But in git_locking the None fallback turns both the per-store git-op lock (`_store_git_op_lock`) and the cross-process `fetch_coordination_lock` into unlocked pass-throughs on Windows. A detached sweep that commits, fetches and pushes on Windows therefore runs with no git-op or fetch serialization, relying only on git's own bounded lock and ref-CAS retries. The plan says "POSIX behaviour is unchanged" but never states this Windows-side degradation.
findings.location: Root cause → "Every module on these paths guards `import fcntl` with a None fallback"; Approach / docs/concurrency.md bullet
scenarios: On Windows a detached sweep's end-of-run push or fetch overlaps a foreground session's fetch on the same common dir. Nothing serializes them, so the loser of git's ref compare-and-swap falls back on retries.
A reviewer reads the fcntl-guard bullet as proof that every lock on the path works on Windows, when two of them become no-ops.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Either route git_locking's git-op and fetch-coordination locks through lock_kernel (msvcrt on Windows), or explicitly state in the plan and in docs/concurrency.md that on Windows the detached sweep runs without rebar's git-op and fetch serialization and relies on git-level retry only.
evidence: git_locking.py:191 `if lock_path is None or fcntl is None: yield; return` (git-op lock is a no-op)
git_locking.py:326 `if common is None or fcntl is None: yield; return` (fetch-coordination lock is a no-op)
git_locking.py docstring: the per-store lock exists because 'git ops also run outside [the store write lock] (sync/push fetch-merge legs...)'
janitor.run_gc, by contrast, uses lock_kernel.take_exclusive, which has an msvcrt leg
findings.finding: The plan cites 'Every module on these paths guards `import fcntl` with a None fallback (lock_kernel, git_locking, repo_snapshot)' as evidence that the sweep is safe on Windows. But in git_locking the None fallback does not mean 'works on Windows'. It means 'runs unlocked'. When fcntl is None, `_store_git_op_lock` and `fetch_coordination_lock` just yield without taking any lock. This change starts a background sweep that commits, fetches and pushes on every eligible Windows close, running alongside foreground rebar git operations. Those operations then have no rebar-level serialization, and the only protection left is the bounded git lock retry or ref-CAS retry. The plan does not acknowledge this, and the docs (concurrency.md) present 'no rebar-git-op.lock' sharing as part of the sweep's isolation story.
findings.location: Root cause bullet 'Every module on these paths guards `import fcntl` with a None fallback'; src/rebar/_store/git_locking.py
scenarios: On Windows, a detached sweep's end-of-run push or fetch races a foreground `rebar sync` fetch on the shared common dir. Neither holds rebar-fetch.lock, so one fails with 'cannot lock ref' and has to rely on the CAS retry.

On Windows, a sweep commit and a foreground commit outside the store write lock contend on index.lock with no advisory git-op lock. Under sustained contention this can use up the ~21 s retry budget and fail a write.

findings.finding: The plan has the docs say Windows 'detaches the same way' and keeps the flags unchanged (DETACHED_PROCESS | CREATE_NO_WINDOW). These flags are not equivalent to POSIX start_new_session. DETACHED_PROCESS only detaches the child from the console. The child stays in the parent's Windows job object, so a launcher, CI runner, IDE or agent harness that runs commands in a kill-on-close job will terminate the sweep when that job closes. That can happen mid-fold or mid-push. The plan does not reason about this case, so the claim of the same lifetime as POSIX is unverified.
findings.location: Approach: '`src/rebar/_proc.py`: correct the `_detach_kwargs` docstring ... Flags unchanged' and the docs bullet 'now say Windows detaches the same way'
scenarios: A CLI close run inside a tool that wraps child processes in a kill-on-close job object. The sweep is killed as soon as that tool's job ends, often in the middle of a fold, leaving recovery to the intent journal and a stale lock to stale-lock reclaim.
A Windows CI step ends. The runner's job cleanup kills the detached GC or sweep worker partway through a pass.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Check the nt detach flags against Microsoft's process-creation-flags docs (CREATE_NO_WINDOW is ignored with DETACHED_PROCESS) and change `_detach_kwargs` so the detached child's git subprocesses open no console windows. evidence: Plan: "`rebar._proc._detach_kwargs` already returns `DETACHED_PROCESS | CREATE_NO_WINDOW` on nt, but is documented as 'not reached in v1'" and "correct the `_detach_kwargs` docstring (the nt branch is now reached). Flags unchanged."

src/rebar/_proc.py:119: `"creationflags": subprocess.DETACHED_PROCESS | subprocess.CREATE_NO_WINDOW`. No other file under src sets creationflags, so the git `subprocess.run` calls in the sweep and GC child (e.g. src/rebar/_snapshot/repo_snapshot.py:347, 538, 560, 578) inherit no window suppression.
Microsoft's process-creation-flags page says CREATE_NO_WINDOW 'is ignored if the application is not a console application, or if it is used with either CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE or DETACHED_PROCESS'.

Hydra PR #172 (retrieved) describes the same combination opening a console window for every console program the detached child later starts. Its fix drops DETACHED_PROCESS in favour of CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | CREATE_NO_WINDOW.
The plan's new Windows test only checks that a marker file is written, so it cannot detect console windows opened by the child's own subprocesses.
findings.finding: The plan keeps `DETACHED_PROCESS | CREATE_NO_WINDOW` ('Flags unchanged'; _proc.py is 'docstring only') and treats `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` as working. Microsoft documents that `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` is ignored when combined with `DETACHED_PROCESS`. The detached sweep and GC child therefore has no console, and every git.exe it starts without creationflags gets a new, visible console window. Several projects document this exact failure (CPython issue 41619, Hydra PR #172, a dev.to write-up). This plan is what first makes the branch reachable for every close and every attested gate on Windows.

scenarios: A Windows user runs `rebar close`. The background sweep starts, and each git call it makes flashes a console window on the desktop.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Cover job objects in the Windows detach design (detect the parent's job and add CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB when it allows breakaway, or document the limitation). Make the e2e test prove the child outlives an intermediate parent process that exits, not just the still-running pytest process.
evidence: Plan: "a real `spawn_detached` child (DETACHED_PROCESS | CREATE_NO_WINDOW) runs after the parent returns and writes a marker file … That is the end-to-end proof that the nt detach branch works." The 'parent' here is the test process, which does not exit.
grep of src for 'BREAKAWAY' returns no matches, so no breakaway handling exists.

Microsoft Q&A (retrieved): if the caller's handle was the last one to the job, closing it triggers JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE and the system terminates every process in the job. Child processes are not otherwise terminated just because their parent exits.

Microsoft's Job Objects docs (retrieved): children are left out of the job only if it sets JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_BREAKAWAY_OK and the parent passes CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB, or if it sets SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK.
Cortex PR #739 (retrieved) adds CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB only when the measured job allows it, and notes that behaviour inside real hook processes on Windows is unmeasured.
findings.finding: The plan does not consider Windows job objects. A process started with `DETACHED_PROCESS` stays in its parent's job. If the parent is in a job with `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE`, Windows kills the sweep or GC child when the CLI exits and the last handle to the job closes. This happens with many IDE, terminal, agent-host and CI launchers. Prior art handles this case with `CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB`, used only when the job allows breakaway. The planned end-to-end proof does not exercise it: it checks the child 'runs after the parent returns' while the pytest parent process is still alive.
findings.location: Approach → New tests in `tests/unit/test_detached_maintenance_windows.py` (Windows-only spawn_detached marker test); Approach → `_detach_kwargs` 'Flags unchanged'
scenarios: `rebar close` runs from a terminal, IDE or agent host that wraps commands in a kill-on-close job. The CLI exits, the job closes and the sweep dies mid-run, leaving its stamped worker lock to be reclaimed later.
The CI or validation run passes because pytest outlives the child, but real CLI invocations under a job never complete a fold.

Evidence class: Unverified. This is based on Win32 CreateProcess console-allocation semantics and has not been observed on a runner. The plan does no probe of it.
findings.finding: Microsoft's process-creation-flags documentation says CREATE_NO_WINDOW is ignored when combined with DETACHED_PROCESS, so the plan's claim about 'DETACHED_PROCESS | CREATE_NO_WINDOW' needs checking. More importantly, a DETACHED_PROCESS python has no console, so each console-subsystem grandchild it starts (the sweep's git commands, for example) may be given a new, visible console window unless those calls pass CREATE_NO_WINDOW. No call site in src/rebar does that. The plan's marker test does not start any grandchild, so this is never exercised.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the invariant that retire's sweep-stop protects on POSIX. Explain why a sweep that keeps running past retire is still safe on Windows, given that the write lock is released only per ticket boundary. evidence: "So on Windows a retire lets the sweep run on instead of stopping it. The docstring says so."
"No config key... POSIX behaviour is unchanged" (POSIX keeps stopping the sweep, implying the stop exists for a reason)
findings.finding: On Windows, retire now lets a running sweep continue instead of stopping it. The plan argues this is acceptable because the retiring server's finish() waits on the store write lock, which the sweep releases at each ticket boundary. That only delays the retiring server until the next boundary. After that, the old sweep keeps folding tickets while the successor server runs, possibly on a newer code version after an upgrade. The plan does not say why POSIX stops the sweep on retire, or why that invariant is safe to drop on Windows.
findings.location: Approach > compact_trigger.py (stop_local_sweep and retiring server finish() bullets)
scenarios: A rebar upgrade on Windows retires the old server while a sweep spawned by the old version is mid-run. The old sweep and the new server then interleave writes to the store, possibly with different on-disk formats.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a Windows contention probe: hold the store write lock in a detached child for more than 15 s and assert that a foreground writer waits and then succeeds (no OSError). evidence: "`rebar._store.lock_kernel` has had a Windows (`msvcrt`) leg since 035b7371de8"
The 13 tests observe 'no inline fold and no spawn (`assert []`, `0 == 1`)', which is spawn counting, not contention.
findings.finding: The plan makes concurrent store-lock contention reachable on Windows for the first time: a detached sweep or GC worker holding the msvcrt-based store lock while a foreground CLI or server writes. The only evidence for the Windows lock leg is that it 'has existed since 035b7371de8'. msvcrt.locking LK_LOCK retries for about 10 s and then raises instead of blocking. Neither the 13 tests nor the new tests are described as exercising contention between a running sweep and a foreground writer.

scenarios: A sweep folds a large ticket for more than 10 s while the user runs another `rebar` write. On Windows the foreground lock attempt raises instead of waiting, or the retiring server's finish() fails.

findings.finding: The plan changes Windows retire semantics. stop_local_sweep no longer signals, the sweep runs on, and the retiring server's finish() waits on the store write lock until the sweep releases it at a ticket boundary. Yet the only planned test asserts that no signal is sent. Nothing verifies that a retire on Windows with a live sweep holding the write lock actually completes, rather than hanging or starving, or that the sweep's later writes stay serialized with the successor.
